short_definition: Confirmation bias is the tendency to search for, notice, interpret and remember information in ways that support what we already believe, while discounting evidence that contradicts it.
explanation: Confirmation bias mostly works on autopilot. Once you hold a view, you tend to ask leading questions, follow sources that agree with you, give supporting evidence the benefit of the doubt and pick apart anything that doesn't fit. Social media feeds can make this worse by showing you more of what you already engage with.

Confirmation bias quietly distorts big decisions about money, hiring, health, relationships and business ideas. With money, it can lead people to hold onto a losing investment because they only read positive commentary, or to ignore warning signs in a too-good-to-be-true offer. In business, founders may hear only the customer feedback that supports their plan.

You can't switch confirmation bias off, but you can build habits that counter it. Before you look at evidence, write down what would change your mind. Seek out the strongest opposing argument, or ask someone to play devil's advocate. Keep a decision journal so you can compare what you expected with what actually happened. These habits take time and can feel uncomfortable, which is their main cost.
example: Example (illustrative numbers): Priya has already decided to buy a Brand A laptop. She reads ten reviews: eight praise it, and two report battery problems, which she dismisses as 'probably faulty units.' A better approach: before reading, she writes, 'If 2 or more of 10 independent reviews report battery failure, I'll seriously consider Brand B.' Committing in advance makes the two negative reviews count.
common_mistake: Believing that being smart or well-informed protects you from it. More knowledge can simply make you better at finding arguments for what you already think.
title: Confirmation Bias
